workdays.title: Revenue & Refund Investigation
workdays.briefing: Revenue is up, refund complaints are up faster, and the CEO wants to know whether growth quality is deteriorating before the afternoon review.
workdays.datasetName: ec_case_customers + ec_case_order_events + ec_case_refund_events (SQLite clean view: ec_case_clean_orders)
issueOptions: Duplicate order events need a latest-event-per-order policy before summing revenue.
Refund events must be deduplicated by refund_id, and cancelled/fully refunded orders excluded from recognized revenue.
Mixed timezone timestamps must be normalized before day-level trend comparisons.
Every high-value order should be deleted automatically as an outlier.
Growth is proven because the largest segment has the most completed revenue.
correctIssues: Duplicate order events need a latest-event-per-order policy before summing revenue.
Refund events must be deduplicated by refund_id, and cancelled/fully refunded orders excluded from recognized revenue.
Mixed timezone timestamps must be normalized before day-level trend comparisons.
workdays.analysisPrompt: Work with the case's real SQLite tables. Use ec_case_clean_orders (latest order update + unique refund records) JOIN ec_case_customers, filter status = 'completed', and return exactly segment and SUM(net_revenue) AS revenue. The result must reconcile to actual data, not hardcoded numbers.
workdays.statisticsPrompt: Enterprise contributes the most *net recognized revenue* in this one-period case. What can the evidence establish, and what would require additional periods or cost data?
statisticsOptions: Enterprise leads this snapshot at ₹9,550, but that does not prove higher growth or profitability; compare periods, returns and contribution margin before acting.
Enterprise customers definitely cause growth and profitable retention.
Delete all other segments because they are smaller.
One snapshot establishes a month-over-month improvement.
workdays.statisticsExpected: Enterprise leads this snapshot at ₹9,550, but that does not prove higher growth or profitability; compare periods, returns and contribution margin before acting.
workdays.chartPrompt: Which decision-ready dashboard view will reveal both segment mix and genuine changes in returns over time?
chartOptions: Segment net-revenue bars with refund/return context, plus properly defined period trends once more periods are available.
A 3D pie chart without labels.
A total gross-revenue gauge that ignores refunds.
A trend line inferred from one aggregated snapshot.
workdays.chartExpected: Segment net-revenue bars with refund/return context, plus properly defined period trends once more periods are available.
workdays.managerPrompt: Write 2–4 sentences to the CEO: cite the checked net revenue figures (Enterprise ₹9,550, Consumer ₹3,400, SMB ₹3,400), explain the snapshot limitation, and recommend how to validate refunds, margin and growth over time.
workdays.managerReference: Enterprise has ₹9,550 in net recognized revenue versus ₹3,400 each for Consumer and SMB, from ₹16,350 total in this synthetic order snapshot after order/refund-event deduplication. This does not prove revenue growth or profitability because we lack comparable prior periods and complete costs. I recommend checking the return and contribution-margin trends by segment across matched periods before adjusting commercial spend.
workdays.reviewFeedback: Your investigation used a versioned, full synthetic order/refund-event dataset and a real SQL validation step; explain uncertainty and export the reproducible data, query and audit evidence.
workdays.resumeBullet: Analyzed a synthetic e-commerce order/refund dataset using SQL deduplication, net-revenue reconciliation, segment comparison and a qualified executive recommendation.

workdays.title: Retention & MRR Investigation
workdays.briefing: Leadership sees rising MRR but customer success reports churn. Determine what the active revenue base looks like and avoid hiding churn through survivorship bias.
issueOptions: Looking only at currently active accounts creates survivorship bias for churn analysis.
MRR and logo retention answer different questions and should both be tracked.
Cohort/segment mix can change the aggregate retention story.
Inactive accounts should be deleted before any retention analysis.
NRR above 100% means no customer churn occurred.
correctIssues: Looking only at currently active accounts creates survivorship bias for churn analysis.
MRR and logo retention answer different questions and should both be tracked.
Cohort/segment mix can change the aggregate retention story.
workdays.analysisPrompt: Calculate September active MRR by segment. Keep the inactive/churned account visible in your reasoning even though active MRR excludes it. If you choose SQL, return exactly segment and SUM(mrr) AS active_mrr.
workdays.statisticsPrompt: If you report only active September accounts, what is the main analytical risk?
statisticsOptions: Survivorship bias: churned/inactive accounts disappear from the retained sample and can make retention look healthier.
There is no risk because inactive accounts are irrelevant.
The only issue is chart color.
The sample becomes randomized automatically.
workdays.statisticsExpected: Survivorship bias: churned/inactive accounts disappear from the retained sample and can make retention look healthier.
workdays.chartPrompt: Which view best supports a retention decision?
chartOptions: Cohort retention heatmap plus segment MRR/NRR context.
A single total-MRR KPI card only.
A pie chart for every month.
A gauge for number of support tickets.
workdays.chartExpected: Cohort retention heatmap plus segment MRR/NRR context.
workdays.managerPrompt: Explain to the Head of Product whether MRR growth proves retention health. Use evidence, a limitation and a next step.
workdays.managerReference: September active MRR is concentrated in Enterprise at ₹9,800, with MidMarket ₹2,800 and SMB ₹1,200, while at least one SMB account is inactive. MRR growth alone does not establish healthy retention because inactive accounts and cohort mix can be hidden. I recommend tracking logo retention and cohort NRR beside active MRR and segmenting churn by plan/tenure.
workdays.reviewFeedback: You separated recurring-revenue growth from retention health and explicitly handled survivorship bias.
workdays.resumeBullet: Analyzed SaaS active MRR and retention risk by segment while identifying survivorship bias and cohort-mix limitations.

workdays.title: Credit Risk Portfolio Review
workdays.briefing: Risk committee sees the delinquency ratio move while the loan book grows. Quantify exposure and challenge a proposal to use a convenient proxy as a hard decision rule.
issueOptions: A falling risk ratio can coexist with rising absolute risky exposure if the denominator grows faster.
A review/risk flag is not proof of wrongdoing or default.
Sensitive customer attributes should be minimized and governed.
A correlated proxy can be used as a definitive policy without validation.
Absolute exposure never matters if the ratio improves.
correctIssues: A falling risk ratio can coexist with rising absolute risky exposure if the denominator grows faster.
A review/risk flag is not proof of wrongdoing or default.
Sensitive customer attributes should be minimized and governed.
workdays.analysisPrompt: Calculate total outstanding exposure by risk_band. If you choose SQL, return exactly risk_band and SUM(outstanding) AS exposure.
workdays.statisticsPrompt: The High-risk share falls after the total loan book expands, but High-risk rupees rise. What should committee hear?
statisticsOptions: The ratio improved partly because the denominator grew; evaluate both absolute exposure and the ratio before declaring lower risk.
The portfolio is definitely safer because the ratio fell.
Only absolute exposure matters and ratios are useless.
Delete all High-risk loans from the analysis.
workdays.statisticsExpected: The ratio improved partly because the denominator grew; evaluate both absolute exposure and the ratio before declaring lower risk.
chartOptions: Exposure by risk band with both amount and share, plus delinquency trend.
One pie chart showing only current share.
A decorative map unrelated to credit risk.
A gauge with no denominator definition.
workdays.chartExpected: Exposure by risk band with both amount and share, plus delinquency trend.
workdays.managerPrompt: Write a risk-committee note that quantifies exposure, explains the denominator issue, avoids treating risk flags as guilt, and recommends a governed next step.
workdays.managerReference: High-risk exposure is ₹500k versus ₹2.42M Low and ₹45k Medium in this snapshot. A lower High-risk ratio can still reflect denominator growth rather than lower absolute risk, and review flags are not proof of default. I recommend monitoring both rupee exposure and share, validating any proposed proxy, and keeping customer-level decisions inside approved governance controls.
workdays.reviewFeedback: You combined portfolio measurement with denominator awareness and governance judgment.
workdays.resumeBullet: Delivered a credit-risk portfolio review combining exposure aggregation, denominator-aware interpretation and governance-safe recommendations.

workdays.title: Wait-Time & Capacity Investigation
workdays.briefing: Leadership says overall wait time improved, but weekend complaints remain high. Determine whether mix effects are hiding unit-level performance and prepare an operational capacity recommendation.
issueOptions: An overall average can improve even if subgroup performance worsens when the mix of units changes.
Weekend/day mix should be checked before attributing the change to staffing.
Tail wait metrics can remain poor even if the median improves.
An overall average always tells the complete operational story.
Any association after a staffing change proves staffing caused it.
correctIssues: An overall average can improve even if subgroup performance worsens when the mix of units changes.
Weekend/day mix should be checked before attributing the change to staffing.
Tail wait metrics can remain poor even if the median improves.
workdays.analysisPrompt: Calculate average wait minutes by unit across the observed hospital_daily_ops rows. If you choose SQL, return exactly unit and ROUND(AVG(avg_wait_minutes), 1) AS avg_wait.
workdays.statisticsPrompt: Overall wait falls while one unit worsens and its share of visits shrinks. What phenomenon should you check?
statisticsOptions: Simpson's paradox / composition effect: the aggregate can move differently from subgroup trends.
The central limit theorem proves staffing worked.
Survivorship bias always explains the result.
A lower overall average means every unit improved.
workdays.statisticsExpected: Simpson's paradox / composition effect: the aggregate can move differently from subgroup trends.
chartOptions: Unit-level wait trends with median/P90 and a capacity-gap view by day.
One overall average KPI only.
A pie chart of wait minutes.
A scatter plot with unit names as numeric values.
workdays.chartExpected: Unit-level wait trends with median/P90 and a capacity-gap view by day.
workdays.managerPrompt: Write the operations lead a concise note separating aggregate and unit-level evidence, mentioning composition/causal limits, and recommending a capacity action.
workdays.managerReference: Emergency averages about 59 minutes versus 30 for Outpatient, so the aggregate should not be interpreted without unit mix. A change in patient mix can create a Simpson's-paradox-style aggregate improvement even if a subgroup worsens, and timing alone does not prove staffing caused the change. I recommend monitoring median/P90 by unit and adding weekend capacity where forecast demand exceeds plan.
workdays.reviewFeedback: You diagnosed a composition effect instead of trusting one aggregate and translated it into an operational capacity decision.
workdays.resumeBullet: Investigated hospital wait-time and capacity performance using subgroup analysis, composition-effect reasoning and operational recommendations.

workdays.title: SLA & Cost Efficiency Investigation
workdays.briefing: Average shipment cost rose and late deliveries are concentrated on a few routes. Determine whether cost efficiency truly worsened after accounting for shipment weight and route mix.
issueOptions: Absolute shipping cost should be normalized by workload such as weight when judging efficiency.
Route mix can change network averages even if route-level efficiency is unchanged.
Promised and actual timestamps/hours must use consistent time definitions.
The most expensive route should automatically be cut.
A lower cost/kg proves total company profit increased.
correctIssues: Absolute shipping cost should be normalized by workload such as weight when judging efficiency.
Route mix can change network averages even if route-level efficiency is unchanged.
Promised and actual timestamps/hours must use consistent time definitions.
workdays.analysisPrompt: Calculate shipping cost per kilogram by route using total cost / total weight. If you choose SQL, return exactly route_code and ROUND(SUM(shipping_cost) / SUM(weight_kg), 2) AS cost_per_kg.
workdays.statisticsPrompt: Average cost rises while average shipment weight rises faster and cost/kg falls. What is the strongest interpretation?
statisticsOptions: Absolute cost increased, but normalized shipping efficiency improved; investigate weight and route mix before cutting spend.
Efficiency definitely worsened because average cost rose.
Cost/kg falling proves total profit increased.
Weight should be ignored because it is not revenue.
workdays.statisticsExpected: Absolute cost increased, but normalized shipping efficiency improved; investigate weight and route mix before cutting spend.
workdays.chartPrompt: Which network view best supports action?
chartOptions: Route-level cost/kg and SLA bars plus a time trend for late-rate/P90 transit time.
One total shipping-cost gauge.
A pie chart of route names.
A map with no metrics or labels.
workdays.chartExpected: Route-level cost/kg and SLA bars plus a time trend for late-rate/P90 transit time.
workdays.managerPrompt: Write the Network Director a note explaining absolute vs normalized cost, route/SLA context, uncertainty, and the next operational investigation.
workdays.managerReference: Route cost/kg ranges from about ₹32.20 on SN-1 to ₹35.70 on WE-1, so higher absolute shipment cost should not be read as lower efficiency without workload normalization. Route and weight mix can move the network average, and cost/kg alone does not explain lateness. I recommend pairing cost/kg with SLA/P90 by route and investigating capacity and carrier handoffs on the late routes.
workdays.reviewFeedback: You normalized cost, protected against route-mix distortion and connected efficiency to SLA rather than optimizing cost alone.
workdays.resumeBullet: Analyzed logistics SLA and normalized route cost efficiency using workload-adjusted metrics and decision-ready network recommendations.

domainPlaybooks.title: E-commerce Business Playbook
domainPlaybooks.operatingModel: Traffic becomes orders through conversion; orders become revenue through basket size; revenue becomes contribution through margin, returns and fulfilment economics.

metrics.name: GMV
metrics.formula: Sum of merchandise value before selected deductions
metrics.trap: GMV is not the same as recognized/net revenue.

metrics.name: Net Revenue
metrics.formula: Gross sales - returns/refunds/discounts according to policy
metrics.trap: Definition must be consistent across Finance and Product.

metrics.name: Conversion
metrics.formula: Orders or purchasers / eligible visits or users
metrics.trap: Wrong denominator can make a good channel look bad or vice versa.

metrics.name: AOV
metrics.trap: Can rise because low-value customers disappeared.

metrics.name: Gross Margin %
metrics.trap: Revenue growth with falling margin can be unhealthy.

metrics.name: Return Rate
metrics.formula: Returned orders or value / eligible orders or value
metrics.trap: Mix shifts can change the rate without product quality changing.

domainPlaybooks.title: SaaS Business Playbook
domainPlaybooks.operatingModel: Acquire accounts, activate users, retain recurring revenue, expand healthy customers and manage churn/contraction.

metrics.name: MRR
metrics.formula: Recurring monthly revenue under the company's policy
metrics.trap: MRR growth can hide logo churn or concentration.

metrics.name: ARR
metrics.formula: Usually MRR × 12 when policy is stable
metrics.trap: Not the same as GAAP/recognized annual revenue.

metrics.name: GRR
metrics.trap: Expansion cannot rescue GRR.

metrics.name: NRR
metrics.trap: >100% does not mean zero churn.

metrics.name: CAC
metrics.trap: Attribution window and included spend matter.

metrics.name: Payback
metrics.formula: CAC / monthly gross profit per customer
metrics.trap: Revenue-only payback overstates economics if gross margin is low.

domainPlaybooks.title: Banking / Risk Playbook
domainPlaybooks.operatingModel: Grow deposits/loans and transaction activity while managing credit, fraud, liquidity, compliance and customer risk.

metrics.name: Outstanding Exposure
metrics.trap: Do not look only at ratios.

metrics.name: DPD
metrics.trap: A single DPD cut-off can hide migration dynamics.

metrics.name: Gross NPA ratio
metrics.trap: Ratio can fall while absolute NPA rises if denominator grows faster.

metrics.name: Review Rate
metrics.trap: Review flag is not proof of fraud.

metrics.name: Net Interest Margin
metrics.formula: Net interest income / average earning assets
metrics.trap: Needs funding-cost and balance-sheet context.

metrics.name: Cost-to-Income
metrics.trap: Aggressive cost cuts can degrade control/service.

domainPlaybooks.title: Hospital Operations Playbook
domainPlaybooks.operatingModel: Balance arrivals, capacity, throughput and service reliability while keeping analytics operational—not clinical—unless appropriately governed.

metrics.name: Median Wait
metrics.trap: Can improve while severe tail waits remain bad.

metrics.name: P90 Wait
metrics.trap: Needs sufficient sample and consistent start/end definitions.

metrics.name: Utilization
metrics.trap: Very high utilization can reduce resilience.

metrics.name: Throughput
metrics.trap: Volume alone does not measure quality.

metrics.name: Cancellation Rate
metrics.trap: Mix and policy changes affect comparability.

metrics.name: Capacity Gap
metrics.trap: Forecast uncertainty should be explicit.

domainPlaybooks.title: Logistics Business Playbook
domainPlaybooks.operatingModel: Move shipments through a network while balancing SLA, capacity, route/carrier mix, utilization and unit cost.

metrics.name: On-time SLA
metrics.formula: On-time delivered shipments / eligible delivered shipments
metrics.trap: Define promised threshold consistently.

metrics.name: P90 Transit
metrics.trap: Average can hide severe late shipments.

metrics.name: Cost/kg
metrics.trap: May still need distance/service-level normalization.

metrics.name: Warehouse Utilization
metrics.trap: Near-100% can hurt flow and resilience.

metrics.name: Throughput Gap
metrics.trap: Forecast error requires scenarios.

metrics.name: Exception Rate
metrics.trap: Route mix and exception definitions matter.

leadershipCases.title: Junior analyst ships a causal claim
leadershipCases.context: A junior writes: “Training caused retention to rise because trained accounts retained 12 pp better.” The analysis is observational and larger accounts were more likely to attend training.

choices.text: Approve it because the difference is large.
choices.feedback: Effect size does not remove confounding.

choices.text: Coach them to state association, identify account-size confounding and propose adjustment or an experiment.
choices.feedback: Senior-quality review: preserve useful evidence while fixing the causal overclaim.

choices.text: Delete the analysis and report nothing.
choices.feedback: You avoided overclaiming but failed to salvage the descriptive evidence.

leadershipCases.title: Two analysts need your help
leadershipCases.context: One analyst has a cosmetic dashboard formatting issue. Another has a many-to-many join inflating board revenue by 18%. You have 30 minutes.

choices.text: Fix the revenue join first, document the grain issue, then delegate formatting.
choices.feedback: Prioritize decision risk and materiality.

choices.text: Fix the dashboard formatting because executives will see it.
choices.feedback: Visibility does not outrank a material metric defect.

choices.text: Split time evenly and finish neither.
choices.feedback: Equal time is not the same as good prioritization.

leadershipCases.title: Quarter analytics roadmap
leadershipCases.context: You can fund two initiatives: rebuild metric definitions, add 20 decorative dashboard pages, automate recurring data-quality checks, or build an unvalidated prediction model.

choices.text: Metric definitions + automated data-quality checks.
choices.feedback: Strong foundational investment: trustworthy metrics and repeatable controls increase leverage across the team.

choices.text: 20 dashboard pages + prediction model.
choices.feedback: Breadth without governance increases maintenance and decision risk.

choices.text: Prediction model + dashboard pages because they look innovative.
choices.feedback: Innovation without reliable inputs/definitions is fragile.

leadershipCases.title: Sales and Finance use different revenue
leadershipCases.context: Sales wants bookings, Finance wants recognized revenue, and leadership keeps asking why dashboards disagree.

choices.text: Create a metric contract that names both metrics, owners, grain, timing and intended decisions.
choices.feedback: Good analytics leadership resolves semantic conflict instead of forcing one label onto different concepts.

choices.text: Tell one team to adopt the other's number without documenting meaning.
choices.feedback: This hides rather than resolves the semantic difference.

choices.text: Average both numbers.
choices.feedback: Averaging definitions creates a meaningless metric.

leadershipCases.title: Allocate two analysts
leadershipCases.context: CEO asks for an exploratory AI dashboard; Risk has a regulatory data-quality issue due tomorrow; Product has a low-impact chart request.

choices.text: Put one analyst on the regulatory data-quality issue, one on the CEO exploration with a tight scope; defer the low-impact chart.
choices.feedback: Balanced urgency, risk and strategic value.

choices.text: Put both on the low-impact chart because it is easiest to finish.
choices.feedback: Throughput is not impact.

choices.text: Start all three with both analysts switching constantly.
choices.feedback: Context switching reduces completion and leaves the highest-risk issue exposed.

leadershipCases.title: Executive KPI sprawl
leadershipCases.context: The board pack has 74 KPIs, many with overlapping names and conflicting definitions.

choices.text: Create a tiered KPI dictionary: outcomes, drivers and diagnostics with named owners and retirement rules.
choices.feedback: Head-level governance: reduce noise while preserving drill-down paths.

choices.text: Keep all KPIs because deleting any metric loses information.
choices.feedback: More metrics can reduce decision clarity and increase inconsistency.

choices.text: Let each department define KPIs independently.
choices.feedback: This institutionalizes semantic conflict.

leadershipCases.title: CEO wants speed, CFO wants certainty
leadershipCases.context: CEO wants a churn answer in 10 minutes. CFO refuses any number until every edge case is validated.

choices.text: Provide the approved provisional metric with denominator/window and a confidence label, then schedule the full reconciliation.
choices.feedback: Good executive trade-off: preserve minimum quality while meeting decision speed.

choices.text: Send an unverified number immediately.
choices.feedback: Speed without a quality floor creates avoidable decision risk.

choices.text: Refuse to provide anything for several weeks.
choices.feedback: Maximum certainty can also fail the decision if timing matters.

leadershipCases.title: Sensitive export was shared too broadly
leadershipCases.context: A customer-level risk export with unnecessary contact fields was sent to a wide internal list.

choices.text: Contain access, notify governance/security per policy, preserve audit evidence, minimize future fields and redesign distribution.
choices.feedback: Strong incident response and prevention.

choices.text: Delete the email from your own inbox and say nothing.
choices.feedback: That does not contain the incident or create governance evidence.

choices.text: Rename future files CONFIDENTIAL but keep broad email distribution.
choices.feedback: A filename is not an access control.

leadershipCases.title: Team hits deadlines but errors recur
leadershipCases.context: Delivery speed is high, but metric-definition, join and validation errors keep reappearing.

choices.text: Invest in review checklists, reusable tests, metric contracts and post-mortems; measure escaped defects as well as speed.
choices.feedback: Build a learning system rather than blaming individuals.

choices.text: Add more deadlines so the team becomes faster.
choices.feedback: More pressure can increase error escape rate.

choices.text: Ban all junior analysts from publishing anything.
choices.feedback: Review is necessary, but blocking development does not build team capability.

coachScenarios.title: Defend a causal claim
coachScenarios.prompt: You found conversion is higher for users who saw a new banner. Explain what you can conclude and what you would do next.

coachScenarios.title: Defend median vs mean
coachScenarios.prompt: Your manager asks why you used median order value instead of mean. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

coachScenarios.title: Explain retention health
coachScenarios.prompt: NRR is 104% but logo churn rose. Explain why both can be true and what you would investigate.

coachScenarios.title: Challenge a risk proxy
coachScenarios.prompt: A stakeholder wants to deny service using a feature correlated with review flags. Explain your response.

coachScenarios.title: Explain a capacity forecast
coachScenarios.prompt: Expected Saturday demand is above planned capacity. Explain the recommendation without presenting the forecast as certain.

coachScenarios.title: Explain normalized logistics cost
coachScenarios.prompt: Average shipping cost rose but cost/kg fell. Explain the difference and what you would check next.
